# Vulnerability details

## Impact
On liquidation, the total amount of collateralTokens to be sent to the liquidator is calculated by adding the liquidatorReward (5% of the debt position's `futureValue`) to the debt value in collateral tokens. However, `liquidatorReward` is calculated in `borrowAtokens`, not `collateralTokens`, and is added to the total sum without prior conversion. As a result, the liquidator receives significantly less than the expected reward.

If the liquidator does not set `minimumCollateralProfit`, this will lead to a loss for the liquidator. If `minimumCollateralProfit` is set, the liquidation will fail. If we assume that the frontend automatically sets `minimumCollateralProfit`, this would lead to failed liquidations & accrual of bad protocol debt.

= 125e18 + 100000e6 * 0.05
= 125000000005000000000 Wei
```

When liquidating a borrow position which is overdue or where the owner is under water (below the minimum collateral/debt ratio) the liquidator gets a liquidation bonus for repaying the borrow position. This ensures that the liquidator profits from the liquidation and is incentivised to do it.

The `liquidationReward` is calculated by taking the minimum of two values, the collateral available after deducting the value of the debt and the “normal” liquidatorReward. This is done in case the collateralisation is so low that the “normal” liquidatorReward can not be payed out.

    assignedCollateral - debtInCollateralToken,
    Math.mulDivUp(debtPosition.futureValue, state.feeConfig.liquidationRewardPercent, PERCENT)
            );
```

For calculating the “normal” liquidatorReward, the `futureValue`(total debt) of the debt position is multiplied by the target `liquidationRewardPercent` and divided by the constant `PERCENT` to adjust the decimals.

The issue arises from the fact that the `futureValue` has 6 decimals (like USDC), the `liquidationRewardPercent` has 18 decimals and `PERCENT` also has 18 decimals. Therefore the “normal” liquidatorReward will always be picked as `liquidatorReward` becasue it is off by 12 decimals and therefore smaller than the remaining collateral value. The first issue is that fees for non-underwater loans are proportional to user's collaterization ratio up to a certain limit. This effectively disincentivizes overcollateralization.

The second issue is that for some liquidation collateral ratios maximum underwater fees can be smaller than maximum non-underwater fees.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-size/blob/8850e25fb088898e9cf86f9be1c401ad155bea86/src/libraries/actions/Liquidate.sol#L90-L100


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Summary: Liquidator reward is severely undermined as it is based off the comparison of two numbers of different types and decimals, ETH in 1e18 and USDC in 1e6, taking the smaller of the two.  

In `executeLiquidate`, liquidatorReward is calculated by fetching the smaller of 2 values, namely:
	1. leftover collateral after repaying the loan (assignedCollateral - debtInCollateralToken)
	2. the debt's future value multiplied by the liquidationRewardPercent (5% in Deploy.sol)
	The issue is that in liquidatorReward calculation should take `debtInCollateralToken` instead of `debtPosition.futureValue` since the latter is denoted in USDC with 6 decimals. 
```solidity
        if (assignedCollateral > debtInCollateralToken) {
            uint256 liquidatorReward = Math.min(
                assignedCollateral - debtInCollateralToken,  // 18 decimals
                Math.mulDivUp(debtPosition.futureValue, state.feeConfig.liquidationRewardPercent, PERCENT) // 6 decimals
            )
    }
    
```
Essentially, the code is comparing two values of different types (ETH-USDC) and different decimals (18-6). If a 1000 USDC loan, backed by 1200 USDC worth of ETH, gets liquidated, the expected reward would be min(200, 50) = 50 USDC (denoted in ETH). However with the current implementation, it will treat the reward as 50e6 ETH or 0.000000000005e18 ETH. If the liquidator had set a minimum expected reward, liquidation will revert. If there was no minimum - liquidator will get essentially nothing, liquidatee will keep a larger portion of their collateral.



## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use `debtInCollateralToken` instead of `debtPosition.futureValue` when calculating liquidatorReward

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-size/blob/main/src/libraries/AccountingLibrary.sol#L256


# Vulnerability details


## Impact

Swap fees are incorrectly calculated when selling partial credit when `exactAmountIn == false`.

## Bug Description

Let's first see the formula for selling partial credit when `exactAmountIn == false`.

https://docs.size.credit/technical-docs/contracts/3.3-market-orders#id-3.3.1.3-technical-specification

The formula is `A = (V+f)*(1+r)/(1-kt)`, where `A` is credit, `V` is amount of cash swapped, `f` is fragmentationFee, `r` is APR, `kt` is swapFeePercentage.

The code uses the same formula to calculate the amount of sold credit by `creditAmountIn = Math.mulDivUp(cashAmountOut + state.feeConfig.fragmentationFee, PERCENT + ratePerTenor, PERCENT - swapFeePercent);`

The total amount of cash that the borrower will receive is `V`, which is `A/(1+r) * (1-kt) - f`.

Let's break down the formula: `A/(1+r)` represents the total cash flow corresponding to the credit. From this, `(1-kt)` percent goes to the borrower, and `kt` percent should be counted as swap fees. Subtract the fragmentationFee `f` from borrower received tokens gives us the original formula.

From the analysis above, the swap fee should be equal to `A/(1+r) * kt`.

However, the current implementation uses `fees = Math.mulDivUp(cashAmountOut, swapFeePercent, PERCENT) + state.feeConfig.fragmentationFee`, which is `V * kt + f = (A/(1+r) * (1-kt) - f) * kt + f`. This is obviously incorrect.

The correct implementation should be `fees = Math.mulDivUp(cashAmountOut + state.feeConfig.fragmentationFee, PERCENT, (1 - swapFeePercent)) - cashAmountOut;`.

## Impact
Any lender that has to claim their loan via multiple fragmented credit positions themselves will still need to pay for the transactions out of their own pocket even though a 'fragmentation fee' has been charged by the protocol.
## Proof of Concept
The protocol collects a fragmentation fee when any credit position is fragmented into 2 or more credit positions. Per the protocol [official documentation](https://docs.size.credit/technical-docs/contracts/2.3-fees#id-2.3.2-fragmentation-fee) at the time of the contest, the fragmentation fee is:

> 
> When a lender sells his credit to a new lender, for example, or uses it as future cash flow to borrow, a new CreditPosition is created in the process.
> 
> Eventually, the new CreditPosition will become liquidity at the due date. However, this new CreditPosition will also have to be claimed (see the claim chapter for more details), which means one additional transaction to be sent on-chain, for each credit fractionalization.
> 
> The Size team intends to run keeper bots to streamline the claim process and aggregate liquidity. However, this operation has some fixed costs in terms of gas, which is why a fixed fee is charged to the user causing the credit split.

If the owner of a credit position, however, claims their position themselves, they'll have to pay for the transaction out of their own pocket. The protocol has collected the fragmentation fee for that operation, but it's keeping it to themselves instead of refunding it to the lender to compensate them for the transaction cost.

The relationship between these values is correctly illustrated in the documentation. 
```
V = A * (1 - k * T) / (1 + r) - f
```

However, when `f` is `0`, `lenders` pay less `cash` than they should, and the protocol receives less `fee` than expected. 
Since the `fee` is the main `revenue source` for the `protocol` and this loss is not ignorable, the impact becomes high. 
And this occurs every time `credit` is sold.

## Impact
The Size protocol uses cross-collateral system, meaning each loan is backed by an amount of collateral that is automatically computed when a "liquidability check" is performed. According to the docs:

"The criteria that is used is the pro rata collateral assignment: since each DebtPosition represents a percentage of the total borrower debt, that loan is backed by an equivalent percentage of the borrower collateral."

The formula used for the automatically assigned collateral for each debt position is:

$$
C_{LB}(t) = \frac{D_{LB}(t)}{D_B(t)} C_B(t) 
$$

with

$$

\begin{array}{l}
  C_B(t) \text{ the total collateral of the borrower } B \text{ at the time } t \\
  D_B(t) \text{ the total debt of the borrower } B \text{ at the time } t \\
  D_{LB}(t) \text{ the total outstanding debt of the loan } L_B \text{ belonging to the borrower } B \text{ at time } t \text{ (amount due to the lenders)} \\
  C_{LB}(t) \text{ the collateral automatically assigned to the loan } L \text{ belonging to the borrower } B \text{ at time } t \\
\end{array}
$$

$$

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Borrowing in Size protocol is a key feature. willing lenders are matched with borrowers. Assuming they have deposited enough collateral, once a borrower finds a willing lender, Borrowers can initiate a sellCreditMarket operation, in which they pay a fee upfront to initiate their borrow position and receive their borrowed tokens.

If they would like to repay their debt, they can do so via the repay function, but only if they repay the entire future value of their debt.
 
However a new feature was added via the compensation mechanism, allowing a borrower to fragment their debt position in order to facilitate partial repayments of their debt. This is because like mentioned earlier, the repayment function only allows full repayment of the debt's future value.

So if we assume a borrower borrows 1 million USDC, and they need to repay 10,000, they can call compensate which will create a new debt position of 10,000 and a credit position linked to it worth 10,000. they can then repay that new debt position and their outstanding loan on their original debt position will then be 990,000. both actions can be combined in a multicall for ease of use.

There are no limits to the number of debt fragments they can generate.
